legends: IMP C C VAL DIOCLETIANVS P F AVG
SACRA MONET AVGG ET CAESS NOSTR
D N DIOCLETIANO BEATISSIMO SEN AVG
coinage.text: Diocletian's coinage falls into two parts. Before 294 he struck reformed radiates in Aurelian's system, with Jupiter, his patron (IOVI CONSERVAT AVGG), and the emperor receiving a globe from Jupiter (CONCORDIA MILITVM). From 294 the reformed system appears: argentei showing the four Tetrarchs sacrificing before a camp gate (VIRTVS MILITVM), and the large follis with GENIO POPVLI ROMANI struck at every mint, alongside SACRA MONET (Moneta with scales) and regional types. Portraits are deliberately uniform, square-jawed and stubbled. After his abdication (1 May 305) coins honour him as 'most blessed senior Augustus' with Quies and Providentia.
coinage.rarity: Folles very common; argentei scarce; aurei scarce to rare.
coinage.confusions: Tetrarchic portraits are near-identical: rely on legends; abdication coins (305-308) are distinct.
coinage.dating: Pre-294 radiates with XXI; 294-305 folles by mint mark sequences (RIC VI).

legends: IMP C M A VAL MAXIMIANVS P F AVG
D N MAXIMIANO BEATISSIMO SEN AVG
coinage.text: Diocletian's co-Augustus took Hercules as his patron (HERCVLI VICTORI, HERCVLI CONSERVAT), and his coins mirror Diocletian's. At Carthage the FELIX ADVENT AVGG NN type marks his African campaign of 297-298. He abdicated in 305, returned in 306-308 alongside his son Maxentius, and after his death at Massilia (310) both Maxentius and Constantine issued consecration coins for him (the latter in 317-318 as part of a 'Divi' series with Constantius I and Claudius II).
coinage.confusions: Galerius also used the name Maximianus (GAL VAL MAXIMIANVS); Maximian's legends read M A VAL or simply MAXIMIANVS, Galerius' include GAL VAL and his portrait is heavier.

legends: IMP C CARAVSIVS P F AVG
coinage.text: The admiral of the Channel fleet who seized Britain and part of northern Gaul struck the first coins made in Britain since the Iron Age, and the most literary coinage of antiquity. Silver denarii of fine metal (rare, the first good silver for decades) carry EXPECTATE VENI, Britannia welcoming the emperor with Aeneas' words to Hector's ghost (Aeneid 2.282-3); the exergual RSR and the medallion letters INPCDA expand into lines from Virgil's Fourth Eclogue ('Redeunt Saturnia regna; iam nova progenies caelo demittitur alto'), as Guy de la Bédoyère showed. Later radiates show him jugate with Diocletian and Maximian (CARAVSIVS ET FRATRES SVI, PAX AVGGG), a bid for recognition. PAX AVG is the commonest type.
coinage.rarity: Radiates scarce to common; denarii rare; aurei very rare; jugate busts rare.
coinage.confusions: Unmarked early radiates and irregular copies; Carausian coins struck for Diocletian and Maximian (with PAX AVGGG and London marks) are Carausian, not central.
coinage.dating: Unmarked early issues (286-c. 290), then ML, L and C marks; jugate issues c. 292.

legends: IMP C ALLECTVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Carausius' finance minister murdered him in 293 and ruled until Constantius' invasion in 296. His coins are neater than Carausius', with a more uniform portrait and the characteristic 'quinarius', a small radiate with a galley reverse (LAETITIA AVG or VIRTVS AVG) and the marks QL or QC. Allectus' gold is very rare. His defeat by Asclepiodotus and Constantius' entry into London are commemorated on the Arras medallion.
coinage.rarity: Radiates scarce; quinarii scarce; aurei very rare.
coinage.confusions: Carausius' issues of similar types.

legends: IMP C L DOMITIVS DOMITIANVS AVG
coinage.text: A usurper in Egypt in 297-298, apparently connected with resistance to Diocletian's new taxes and coinage. He struck both the new Tetrarchic follis (GENIO POPVLI ROMANI, ALE mark) and the old Alexandrian tetradrachm, a revealing mix. His corrector Aurelius Achilleus led the defence of Alexandria during Diocletian's eight-month siege. Rare.
coinage.confusions: Do not confuse with Domitian II of the Gallic Empire.

legends: IMP C CONSTANTIVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Caesar in the West from 293, Augustus from 305 to his death at York in 306. His coins are standard Tetrarchic issues; the outstanding piece is the gold medallion from the Beaurains treasure showing his arrival at London in 296 (REDDITOR LVCIS AETERNAE, 'restorer of the eternal light'). Constantine and Maxentius both issued consecration coins for him (MEMORIA FELIX with altar and eagles; DIVO CONSTANTIO PIO).
coinage.confusions: Constantius II (FL IVL CONSTANTIVS, mid-4th c.) and Constantius Gallus; Constantius I is the only one called NOB CAES on large Tetrarchic folles.

legends: IMP C GAL VAL MAXIMIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Diocletian's Caesar in the East (293-305) and senior Augustus (305-311), victor over Narseh of Persia (298). Officially named Maximianus, he is often confused with Maximian. His capital Thessalonica and later Serdica struck heavily for him; eastern mints introduced GENIO IMPERATORIS and GENIO AVGVSTI variants of the Genius type. His wife Galeria Valeria, Diocletian's daughter, has coins with VENERI VICTRICI (308-311). He died in 311 after his edict of toleration.
coinage.confusions: Legends MAXIMIANVS without GAL VAL may be either Maximian or Galerius; Galerius' coins are mainly eastern, Maximian's western, and Galerius as Caesar is NOB C.

legends: IMP C FL VAL SEVERVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Galerius' choice as western Caesar in 305 and Augustus after Constantius' death in 306. His invasion of Italy against Maxentius collapsed in 307 when his troops deserted, and he was captured and forced to commit suicide. His folles are standard Tetrarchic types. As Augustus his coinage is scarcer than as Caesar.
coinage.confusions: Septimius Severus (2nd-3rd c.) has entirely different coins.

legends: IMP C GAL VAL MAXIMINVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Galerius' nephew, Caesar in the East from 305, given the compromise title 'son of the Augusti' (filius Augustorum) in 309-310 before taking the rank of Augustus. His coins reflect his pagan revival in the East: Sol Invictus, Genius types, and at Antioch SOLI INVICTO with Sol holding Serapis' head. Defeated by Licinius in 313, he died at Tarsus. The FIL AVGG coins (also issued for Constantine) document the short-lived attempt to manage four emperors' rivalries.
coinage.confusions: Maximinus vs Maximianus: read carefully.

legends: IMP C MAXENTIVS P F AVG
DIVO ROMVLO N V BIS CONS
coinage.text: Son of Maximian, proclaimed in Rome in October 306. He first called himself princeps invictus, then Augustus. Unlike the clean-shaven Constantine, he is bearded. His coins centre on the city of Rome: Roma in her hexastyle temple (CONSERV VRB SVAE), the Dioscuri (AETERNITAS AVG N), the she-wolf with twins, and the domed shrine of his dead son Romulus (AETERNAE MEMORIAE). Ostia's coins are especially fine. Defeated at the Milvian Bridge (28 October 312), he suffered damnatio memoriae.
coinage.rarity: Folles common; Divus Romulus scarce; gold rare.
coinage.confusions: Folles of Maxentius for Maximian and Constantius I (consecration) bear their names.

legends: S P Q R OPTIMO PRINCIPI
coinage.text: The vicarius of Africa, proclaimed by the troops after refusing to send his son as hostage to Maxentius. His folles from Carthage (PK marks) celebrate Carthage and Rome together; gold is very rare. Maxentius' praetorian prefect crushed him c. 310 and sacked Carthage and Cirta. A favourite target of forgers.
coinage.confusions: Fakes are common; check against die studies.

legends: IMP C VAL LICIN LICINIVS P F AVG
D N VAL LICIN LICINIVS NOB C
coinage.text: Made Augustus at Carnuntum (308), Licinius ruled the Danube and, after defeating Maximinus Daia (313), the whole East. His coinage stays loyal to Jupiter: the standard eastern type of 313-324 is IOVI CONSERVATORI with Jupiter holding Victory on a globe, an eagle at his feet with a wreath and sometimes a captive. Eastern gold shows Licinius and his son Licinius II in facing portraits with large square heads, an innovation. Licinius II, Caesar from 317 as a baby, appears on many folles. After his defeats at Adrianople and Chrysopolis (324) and his execution (325), his memory was condemned.
coinage.confusions: Licinius I vs II by legend (AVG vs NOB C); Licinius' western issues before 316-317 share Constantinian types.
coinage.dating: 308-324; issues by mint marks and VOT numbers.

legends: IMP C AVR VAL VALENS P F AVG
D N M MARTINIANO P F AVG
coinage.text: Licinius twice tried to strengthen his position by raising a subordinate to Augustus. Aurelius Valerius Valens, a frontier commander, was proclaimed in 316 during the first war with Constantine and sacrificed at the peace of 317. Martinianus, his magister officiorum, was raised in 324 before Chrysopolis and executed afterwards. Both struck only briefly at eastern mints with Jupiter types. Their coins are very rare and much forged.
coinage.confusions: Valens of 316 is unrelated to the emperor Valens (364-378).

coinage.text: Constantine's 31-year coinage moves from Tetrarchic Genius types (306-310) through Sol Invictus as his companion (to c. 318-320) to the Christian imagery of the 320s-330s, while the solidus he created (c. 309-310) became the backbone of late Roman and Byzantine money. Key series: VICTORIAE LAETAE PRINC PERP (shield on altar, 318-319); VIRTVS EXERCIT with a standard inscribed VOT XX (320); BEATA TRANQVILLITAS (altar with VOTIS XX, 321-324); PROVIDENTIAE AVGG (camp gate, 324-330); GLORIA EXERCITVS (330-337) and the VRBS ROMA and CONSTANTINOPOLIS city coins. From 324-325 he appears with upward gaze and diadem, which Eusebius explains as a pose of prayer. His mother Helena and wife Fausta appear in 324-326 (Fausta disappears after her death in 326). His posthumous coins (337) show him veiled, ascending to heaven in a chariot reaching for the hand of God.
coinage.rarity: Nummi extremely common; solidi available; Helena and Fausta common in bronze; multiples rare.
coinage.confusions: Constantine II as Augustus (337-340) also uses CONSTANTINVS P F AVG and MAX AVG; Constantinopolis/VRBS ROMA city coins have no emperor portrait.
coinage.dating: Weight reductions and type sequences (RIC VI-VII), VOT numbers, and mint marks with fine sub-issue symbols date issues to a year or two.

coinage.text: Constantine's eldest son, Caesar from 317, commander in Gaul against the Franks and Alamanni and admiral in the war with Licinius (324). His coins are very common: laureate or helmeted busts in elaborate armour, with Caesar types (CAESARVM NOSTRORVM, BEATA TRANQVILLITAS, camp gate). In 326 Constantine had him executed at Pola for reasons never explained, and his name was erased from inscriptions.
coinage.confusions: Other Constantinian Caesars (Constantine II, Constantius II, Constans) use similar types: names decide.

legends: FL CL CONSTANTINVS IVN N C
coinage.text: Caesar from 317 as an infant, he ruled the West from Trier as Augustus after 337 and was killed in 340 invading Constans' territory near Aquileia. As Caesar he is IVN (iunior); as Augustus his coins share names with his father's, a common source of error. Gloria Exercitus with one standard (337-340) and Trier and Arles gold of 337-340 are the main Augustus issues.
coinage.rarity: Caesar issues very common; Augustus issues scarcer.
coinage.confusions: Post-337 CONSTANTINVS coins are Constantine II, not his father: check issue marks (e.g. Arles CONST after 337) and the younger portrait.

legends: D N CONSTANS P F AVG
coinage.text: Youngest son of Constantine, Augustus from 337, sole ruler of the West after 340. His common bronzes are VICTORIAE DD AVGGQ NN with two Victories facing each other (341-348). In 348 he and Constantius introduced the FEL TEMP REPARATIO bronze; Constans' types include the emperor on a galley steered by Victory and the phoenix on a pyre or globe. He visited Britain in winter 343, which Firmicus Maternus celebrated. Magnentius overthrew and killed him in 350.
coinage.confusions: Constantius II shares types; check names.

legends: D N CONSTANTIVS P F AVG
coinage.text: The longest-reigning Constantinian (Caesar 324, Augustus 337-361), Constantius ruled the East and, after defeating Magnentius at Mursa (351), the whole empire. His coins are among the commonest of antiquity: GLORIA EXERCITVS, VICTORIAE DD AVGGQ NN, and the FEL TEMP REPARATIO falling horseman of the 350s, followed by the small SPES REIPVBLICE (c. 355-361). Gold shows Roma and Constantinopolis enthroned holding a shield inscribed VOT XX MVLT XXX, and eastern solidi present him in three-quarter view, helmeted with spear and shield, an iconography that anticipates Byzantine gold. Antioch reached 15 officinae for him. His reign saw the reduction of the siliqua (c. 355).
coinage.rarity: Bronze extremely common; solidi and siliquae common for the period.
coinage.confusions: Constantius I (Tetrarchic, NOB CAES on big folles), Constantius Gallus (bare-headed, NOB CAES, 351-354), Constantius III (421): the Flavius Iulius name and diademed bust identify Constantius II.
coinage.dating: VOT numbers (VOT XX, XXV, XXX), mint marks and the shrinking size of the falling horseman type.

coinage.text: Constantine's nephews, raised in 335 as part of his succession plan: Delmatius as Caesar for the Balkans, Hannibalianus as 'king of kings and of the Pontic peoples', destined for Armenia. Delmatius' common GLORIA EXERCITVS nummi are an introduction to the period; Hannibalianus' unique title REX appears on rare nummi with the Euphrates river god reclining (SECVRITAS PVBLICA), struck at Constantinople. Both were killed in the army purge of 337.
coinage.confusions: Spelling DELMATIVS vs DALMATIVS varies by mint.

legends: D N VETRANIO P F AVG
coinage.text: The old magister peditum in Illyricum was proclaimed in March 350, probably at the urging of Constantina, Constantius' sister, to block Magnentius. His bronze carries the first coin legend quoting Constantine's vision, HOC SIGNO VICTOR ERIS ('in this sign you will conquer'), around the emperor holding a labarum. He also struck for Constantius II. In December 350 he abdicated before the troops at Naissus and retired to Prusa with a pension.
coinage.confusions: Constantius' coins struck by Vetranio's mints carry the same types with Constantius' name.

coinage.text: A nephew of Constantine (son of his half-sister Eutropia) who seized Rome in June 350 and held it for 28 days before Magnentius' general Marcellinus killed him. The Rome mint struck a few bronzes and very rare gold, with Roma enthroned. One of the shortest reigns in the coinage.
coinage.confusions: Fakes exist.

legends: D N MAGNENTIVS P F AVG
SALVS DD NN AVG ET CAES
VICTORIAE DD NN AVG ET CAE
coinage.text: An officer of Frankish or British descent who murdered Constans in 350, Magnentius is shown bare-headed and clean-shaven, without the diadem worn by the Constantinians. His most famous coin, a large bronze of 353, has the reverse filled by a chi-rho flanked by alpha and omega (SALVS DD NN AVG ET CAES): either sincere Christianity or a bid for Christian loyalty against Constantius. Common types show two Victories holding a shield inscribed VOT V MVLT X. His Caesar Decentius, perhaps his brother, shares the coinage. Defeated at Mursa (351) and Mons Seleucus (353), both killed themselves.
keyTypes: two Victories VOT V MVLT X
coinage.rarity: Common; large chi-rho scarce; gold scarce.
coinage.confusions: Decentius (NOB CAES) vs Magnentius (AVG).

legends: D N FL CL CONSTANTIVS NOB CAES
D N CONSTANTIVS IVN NOB C
coinage.text: Julian's half-brother, Caesar in the East in 351-354 with his seat at Antioch, where his cruelty became notorious (Ammianus 14). His bronzes are bare-headed FEL TEMP REPARATIO falling horsemen, very common. Constantius had him executed in 354.
keyTypes: FEL TEMP REPARATIO falling horseman (bare head)
coinage.confusions: Constantius II (diademed, AVG).

legends: D N FL CL IVLIANVS NOB CAES
FL CL IVLIANVS P F AVG
D N FL CL IVLIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: As Caesar (355-360) Julian appears bare-headed and beardless. As Augustus (360-363) he is bearded like a philosopher, the beard mocked by the Antiochenes and defended in his satire Misopogon. His large AE1 shows a bull with two stars above (SECVRITAS REIPVB), variously explained as Apis, his own horoscope or a sacrificial victim; Christians took it as a pagan provocation (Socrates HE 3.17). The common AE3 has VOT X MVLT XX in a wreath. His solidi show a soldier dragging a captive (VIRTVS EXERCITVS ROMANORVM).
coinage.rarity: AE3 common; bull AE1 scarce to common; solidi available.
coinage.confusions: Caesar coins of Julian (bare head) vs Gallus (also bare head): names decide.

legends: D N IOVIANVS P F AVG
coinage.text: Chosen by the army after Julian's death in Persia, Jovian made a humiliating peace (ceding Nisibis and Singara) and died in February 364 on the way to Constantinople. His brief coinage restores Christian loyalty and stresses safety: VOT V in a wreath, RESTITVTOR REIP. His AE1 pieces are rare.
coinage.confusions: None.
